entries.text:
Mother Aldith wipes her hands on her apron, takes the leaf between two floury fingers, and reads it standing, with her lips moving slightly. She reads it twice. Then she sniffs and tucks it into her sleeve.

"Edda Thorne. She sent me a letter once telling me I set a wrist wrong. I had. Rot her." It is said with great affection. "Maud Marrow's name counts for something, and I owe her a blanket's worth of favours. I'll see the boy. Have Ansel's lad carry him here before the bread's out of the oven, and mind he doesn't bump the ankle on the way. A crushed ankle wants setting inside a day or two, and the sooner the better."

She jerks her chin at the note. "The girl. Twelve is young, but I started at ten. Can she keep her breakfast down at the sight of bone? Can she count, and hold her tongue? I'll not say yes on paper. Send her with Maud Marrow when the roads are fit, and I'll give her a day at my table and see whether her hands shake. A month's trial is sense. Most folk want a year before they've learned anything."

On the hip, she grunts. "A month-old crooked hip. That's a break-and-reset, if it's the bone, and it's an ugly business. I'll not walk two days for a stubborn dyer. If he wants it straight, he can come to me, and he can bring a bottle of something strong. Tell him so. Tell him it's better than limping to his grave."

She looks you up and down, at the mace, the chain, the soft-handed way you hold the note. "And you? Staying, or off again?"

It is a little before seven. Two of your 1st-level slots are ready, with Channel Divinity. You are 100 XP short of level 3, and the lane outside has begun to smell of the tanneries.

input.add_to_description: Day 6 morning: Brannoc gave her the note for Wren. She agreed to see Tobin's ankle today, will only look at Perrin's hip if he comes to Stonebridge himself, and will meet Wren on a month's trial when Maud brings her. She recognised the Maud Marrow name.

entries.text:
Aldith keeps kneading while you speak. She doesn't look up until you say Maud's name. Then her floury hands stop.

"Maud Marrow." She wipes them on her apron, takes the leaf from you and reads it by the fire, lips moving, holding it at arm's length. It takes her no time at all. "Two lines. Good. I can't abide a letter that wants to be a sermon."

She folds it into her apron pocket. "A twelve-year-old who sweeps a dead chapel because nobody asked her to. Hm. I've had three prentices, and two of them had the sense to stay. A month's trial suits me better than a promise. Have Maud bring her when the roads are dry, and bring a warm blanket, because my loft is cold. If she faints at the sight of bone, she goes home. If she doesn't, we'll see."

Then she turns on the rest, brisk as a slammed door. "The boy first. Ansel's carrying him? Good, I'll have him here by midmorning and look at him on the table. A crushed ankle in a child is better set in the first days than left to knit wrong, and you've done well not to let anyone fuss with it. Tell Ansel to keep it up on a pillow and give him willow-bark tea for the pain."

On Perrin she is blunter. "A hip that healed crooked a month back? I'm not riding to Greywater for any man's pride. If he wants it straight, he walks here, or is carried. I'll tell you now, it means breaking it again, and six weeks flat on his back after. Most of them say no when they hear that. Tell him that plain, and tell him I said the stool was a good start."

Her eyes narrow at your face. "You've not slept enough. Sit. Eat something before you go bothering other people." She pushes a heel of warm bread across the table without waiting for an answer.

It's near half past six. Tobin will be seen today, Wren has a place waiting, and Perrin's choice is his own. You have two 1st-level slots and Channel Divinity ready, and you're 100 XP short of the next level. The valley road runs on south beyond Stonebridge, and you haven't yet heard of any place down it with no healer.

Of Perrin's hip she says the man must come himself; she will not promise to break it again until she has felt it. She wants Brannoc to hold the boy during the setting.

entries.text:
Mother Aldith wipes her hands on her apron, takes the folded leaf between a floury thumb and finger, and reads it standing, lips moving. She reads it twice. Then she snorts.

"Edda's boy. She wrote me once, forty years back, to say I held a splint like a butcher. She was right." She tucks the note into her apron. "Maud Marrow vouches for her, does she? Maud owes me a blanket, not the other way round, but I'll let it pass. A girl who sweeps a dead priest's chapel for nothing has more sense than my last two. Tell her parents a month, and I'll feed her, and she'll hate me by the second week. If Maud brings her, I'll see her. I'll not go to Greywater, mind."

She slaps the dough once and turns to the shelf. "The dyer. Hips that have healed wrong, I can break and set again, but I'll not promise it on a story told by a stranger. He walks in here on his own legs, so I can put my hands on him. Then I'll tell him yes or no. Most don't like it when I say yes."

She is already pulling down splints and a coil of linen. "The boy, now. A crushed ankle, you said, a day old? Then it's high time. I'll want him on my table within the hour, and I'll want someone to hold him still while I work. He'll scream. Ansel's lad is no use. You've the hands and the temper for it, I'd guess. Can you do it?"

She looks you over from boots to amulet and waits.

Wants to see Perrin Gale's hip herself before promising anything, and will meet Wren in person before deciding on an apprentice. Mentions she owes Maud Marrow for winter blankets.

entries.text:
Mother Aldith doesn't stop kneading. She tips her head at the note, and you lay it on the table beside the flour. She wipes one hand on her apron, reads it with her lips pressed thin, and grunts.

"Edda Thorne's boy. She set a collarbone of mine forty years back, and she cursed me the whole time, so I liked her." She reads the second line again. "A dyer's girl who sweeps a chapel nobody asked her to sweep. That's either a fool or a keeper. I'll know which when I see her hands, not when I read a note. Maud's word counts for something, I owe that woman a good many blankets. Send the child down with Maud when the weather holds, and I'll look at her. I promise nothing past looking."

She slaps the dough into a bowl and covers it with a cloth. "A hip healed crooked a month back. That's not old, and it's not new, and it can still be broken and reset if the man has the nerve. Tell your Perrin that. I won't cross the valley for one stubborn dyer, but he can come to me on a cart, and I'll see him. And I'll say it plain: the breaking hurts like the pit, and he'll hate me for a week."

She is already reaching for a leather satchel on the shelf, stuffing in splints and rolls of linen. "The boy with the ankle. Crushed, you say, not broken clean? Those are the ones that go wrong if they wait. I'll come now. Ansel's got hot water, I hope, and not just holy talk."

The air turns colder, and Gorm's breath smokes. Wick reaches for the pole without being told. You said you'd turn back at the first sign of the lights moving.

It's twenty to five on Day 14. You have four 1st-level slots, no 2nd-level slots, and Channel Divinity. The skiff is thirty paces from the south tip. Dusk is under an hour off.

Wick goes white. "That's Jory." He whispers it.

I'll go, but only to scout. "Wick, Gorm, we pole to the south tip, look from the water, and turn back at the first sign of the lights moving. Nobody lands after four-thirty, and nobody goes near that west door."

I'll bring the rope, the hooded lantern, and a few flasks of oil, and keep Shield of Faith ready. I'll watch the bow-mark and the cut reeds for Jory's skiff or any sign of him. DM: can I see from the water whether Jory's skiff is still tied up at the south tip?

entries.text:
Wick Hale poles the skiff with long, quiet strokes, and Gorm sits in the bow with a reed-knife across his knees. You have the rope, the hooded lantern, and three flasks of oil at your feet. The mist closes behind you until the landing is a smudge, and the only sounds are the pole in the water and the hiss of the reeds.

Perception (6): you see very little yourself. The south tip is a wall of grey reeds in the failing light, and to your eyes it is all one colour. Wick, who has cut these reeds for twenty years, sees what you cannot. He lifts two fingers and points without a word.

Jory's skiff is there, pulled up empty in the cut reeds, its painter tied to a stake. A burned-out lantern sits on the thwart, and the two eel-spears are gone. A trail of boot-prints runs from the bow north along the flank of the mound, then bends west, toward the dark gap you saw from the landing. That is as much as the water shows.

You don't linger. When you do hold a moment to look, one of the Wick-fires lifts from the west side and slides a few paces toward you across the reeds, pale and soundless, and the reeds beneath it go grey as ash. Gorm mutters a charm. It is half past four, your own cutoff, and you say turn back. Wick turns the skiff without argument. The light follows you for a little way, then stops and hangs, and you leave it behind in the mist.

You are back at the landing at a quarter past five, with dusk coming on. Ode is waiting at the staithe with her arms folded. You tell her what you saw: the skiff, the trail, the dark door. You say Jory may still be alive, since his boot-prints go toward the mound and not away, and nothing was left to tell otherwise. She hears you out without a word and then nods once.

You have four 1st-level slots, no 2nd-level slots, and Channel Divinity. You can't rest again until tomorrow afternoon at the earliest, as the last long rest ended at half past three today. Dessa and Bram are sleeping easy, and the Long House is quiet.
